t.1.3: Behold, O teacher, this mighty army of the sons of Pāṇḍu, arrayed for battle by the son of Drupada, your wise disciple.
t.1.1: Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: On the field of dharma, on the field of the Kurus, gathered together and eager to fight, what did my sons and the sons of Pāṇḍu do, O Sañjaya?
t.1.4: Here are heroes, mighty archers equal in battle to Bhīma and Arjuna: Yuyudhāna, Virāṭa, and Drupada, the great chariot-warrior.
t.1.2: Saṃjaya said: Then, having seen the army of the Pāṇḍavas drawn up in battle array, King Duryodhana approached his teacher and spoke these words.
t.1.5: Dhṛṣṭaketu, Cekitāna, and the valiant king of Kāśi; Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Śaibya, a bull among men.
t.1.6: The valiant Yudhāmanyu and the mighty Uttamaujā, Saubhadra and the sons of Draupadī, all of them are indeed great chariot-warriors.
t.1.7: But know also those who are most distinguished among us, O best of the twice-born, the leaders of my army; I name them to you for your recognition.
t.1.8: Your honored self, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, and Kṛpa, ever victorious in battle; Aśvatthāmā, Vikarṇa, and likewise the son of Somadatta.
t.1.9: And many other heroes, who have given up their lives for my sake, armed with various weapons and missiles, are all skilled in warfare.
t.1.10: That army of ours, protected by Bhīṣma, is unlimited, whereas this army of theirs, protected by Bhīma, is limited.
t.1.11: Stationed in all the lines of approach, each in his allotted place, all of you, sirs, must guard Bhīṣma above all.
t.1.12: Then the mighty grandsire, the eldest of the Kurus, roared loudly like a lion and blew his conch, bringing joy to him.
t.1.13: Then conchs and kettledrums, tabors, drums and cow-horns were all at once struck up, and that sound became tumultuous.
t.1.14: Then Mādhava and the Pāṇḍava, stationed in a great chariot yoked with white horses, blew their divine conches.
t.1.15: Hṛṣīkeśa blew the Pāñcajanya, Dhanaṃjaya the Devadatta, and Vṛkodara, of terrible deeds, blew the great conch Pauṇḍra.
t.1.16: King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, blew the Anantavijaya, and Nakula and Sahadeva blew the Sughoṣa and the Maṇipuṣpaka.
t.1.17: The king of Kāśī, a supreme archer, and Śikhaṇḍī, the great chariot-warrior, Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Virāṭa, and the unconquered Sātyaki,
t.1.19: That tumultuous uproar, making the sky and the earth resound, rent the hearts of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
t.1.20: Then, seeing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra drawn up in battle array, as the clash of weapons was about to begin, the son of Pāṇḍu, whose banner bore the monkey, raised his bow.
t.1.21: Then, O lord of the earth, he spoke these words to Hṛṣīkeśa: "Place my chariot between the two armies, O Acyuta."
t.1.18: Drupada and the sons of Draupadī, O lord of the earth, and the mighty-armed son of Subhadrā, all of them on every side, blew their conch shells, each his own.
t.1.22: So that I may behold these who stand arrayed, eager to fight, and know with whom I must contend in this undertaking of battle.
t.1.23: I wish to observe those who are about to fight, those who have assembled here, eager to do in battle what is pleasing to the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
t.1.24: Thus addressed by Guḍākeśa, O Bhārata, Hṛṣīkeśa, having stationed the finest of chariots in the middle between the two armies,
t.1.25: In front of Bhīṣma and Droṇa and of all the rulers of the earth, he said: "Pārtha, behold these Kurus assembled here."
t.1.26: There Pārtha saw, standing in place, fathers and also grandfathers, teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, and likewise friends.
t.1.28: Overcome by deep compassion and sinking in despair, he spoke thus: "O Kṛṣṇa, seeing these my own kinsmen standing arrayed here, eager to fight,"
t.1.29: My limbs sink and give way, and my mouth is completely parched; a trembling arises in my body, and my hair stands on end.
t.1.30: Gāṇḍīva slips from my hand, and my skin is burning all over; I am unable to stand steady, and my mind seems to whirl.
t.1.31: And I see adverse omens, O Keśava, nor do I foresee any good in slaying my own kinsmen in battle.
t.1.32: I do not desire victory, O Kṛṣṇa, nor kingdom, nor pleasures. Of what use to us is a kingdom, O Govinda, of what use are enjoyments, or even life itself?
t.1.27: Fathers-in-law and friends as well, in both the armies. Having looked upon all those kinsmen standing arrayed there, the son of Kuntī...
t.1.33: Those for whose sake we desired kingdom, enjoyments and pleasures, these very ones stand here arrayed in battle, having given up their lives and their wealth.
t.1.34: Teachers, fathers, sons, and likewise grandfathers, maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and other kinsmen as well.
t.1.35: These I do not wish to kill, O Madhusūdana, even though they are killing me, not even for the sake of sovereignty over the three worlds; how much less, then, for the sake of the earth?
t.1.36: Having slain the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, what joy could be ours, O Janārdana? Sin alone would cling to us for killing these aggressors.
t.1.37: Therefore we ought not to kill the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra together with their kinsmen; for how could we be happy, O Mādhava, after killing our own people?
t.1.38: Even if these men, their minds overpowered by greed, do not see the wrong caused by the destruction of a family, nor the sin in treachery toward friends.
t.1.39: Why should we not know to turn back from this sin, O Janārdana, we who clearly see the wrong caused by the destruction of a family?
t.1.40: With the destruction of the family, the eternal family dharmas perish; and when dharma is lost, adharma overpowers the entire family.
t.1.41: From the predominance of adharma, O Kṛṣṇa, the women of the family become corrupted; and when the women are corrupted, O Vārṣṇeya, there arises a mixing of varṇas.
t.1.43: By these misdeeds of the destroyers of the family, which bring about the confusion of varṇas, the eternal duties of caste and the duties of the family are destroyed.
t.1.42: This intermixture leads only to hell, for the destroyers of the family and for the family itself; for their ancestors fall, deprived of the rites of offering rice-balls and water.
t.1.44: O Janārdana, we have heard it said that for men whose family dharma has been destroyed, a dwelling in hell is certain.
t.1.45: Alas, alas! We have resolved to commit a great sin, in that, through greed for the pleasures of kingship, we are prepared to slay our own kinsmen.
t.1.46: If the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, weapons in hand, were to slay me in battle, unresisting and unarmed, that would be better for me.
t.1.47: Having spoken thus on the battlefield, Arjuna cast aside his bow together with its arrows and sat down on the seat of the chariot, his mind overwhelmed with grief.
